title: Problem solving: sub-problems, simpler cases and systematic lists
summary: Break a big problem into steps, solve a simpler version first, list every case in order, and choose a strategy yourself.
guide: This studio practises three of the strategies taught in the Iranian Year 2 book: break the problem into smaller steps, solve a simpler problem first, and list every case in order. In the last mission your child chooses the strategy.
Sub-problems: "some problems can be turned into a problem in steps." Your child writes two number sentences; the answer to the first one (the number in the box) joins the numbers for the second one.

Simpler problem: the book suggests using 150 instead of 147 and 10 instead of 11, to see more easily whether to add or subtract. Your child writes a sentence with the easy numbers first, then with the real ones.

Systematic list: your child writes every number in order in a table (all the ones starting with 5 first); the "number" column builds itself. The "why" question at the end of each mission is the look-back step.

sub-problems.title: Sub-problems: pages left
sub-problems.prompt: A storybook has 395 pages. Hassan read 150 pages in the first week and 130 pages in the second week. How many pages has he not read yet? Do it in two steps: a) first work out how many pages he has read; b) then find the pages left.
sub-problems.hint: First sentence: the pages from week one and week two together. Type the number in the box; it then appears among the numbers for the second sentence.
sub-problems.success: Well done! 150 + 130 = 280 pages read. 395 − 280 = 115 pages left.
sub-problems.why: Why did you work out the pages read first? How can you check your answer?
sub-problems.model: To find the pages left I need to know how many he has read altogether; that is a smaller problem. Check: 150 + 130 + 115 = 395, all the pages in the book.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need: all the pages in the book, and the pages from both weeks.
feedback.known-extra: Do you need the number of stories to find the pages?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: 395 pages. What don't we know?
feedback.sentence-empty: Fill every gap in both sentences.
feedback.sentence-box: In each sentence, show the unknown number with one box □.
feedback.sentence-numbers: Step a): add the pages from week one and week two. Step b): take that answer away from 395.
feedback.sentence-false: Read your sentence. Is the sign right?
feedback.solve-empty: Type the number in the box after "□ =".
feedback.solve-wrong: Work out the number in the box again.
feedback.one-week: Hassan read for two weeks. Take away the pages from both weeks.
feedback.added-all: The pages left can't be more than the whole book! Take away the pages he read.
feedback.too-big: Look at the answer to the second sentence.
feedback.too-small: Look at the answer to the second sentence.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

simpler-numbers.title: A simpler problem: Ahmad's height
simpler-numbers.prompt: Reza is 147 cm tall. Ahmad is 11 cm shorter than him. How tall is Ahmad? First use 150 instead of 147 and 10 instead of 11 and solve it. Then use the real numbers.
simpler-numbers.hint: If Reza were 150 cm and Ahmad 10 cm shorter, would Ahmad be more or less than 150? Use the same sign for the real numbers.
simpler-numbers.success: Well done! With easy numbers: 150 − 10 = 140. With the real numbers: 147 − 11 = 136. Ahmad is 136 cm tall.
simpler-numbers.why: How did the easier numbers help you? Why isn't the final answer 140?
simpler-numbers.model: With 150 and 10 I could easily see that "shorter" means subtract: 150 − 10 = 140. Then I did the same with the real numbers: 147 − 11 = 136. 140 was only the simpler problem's answer, but it is close to 136, so my answer makes sense.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need: Reza's height and the difference in height.
feedback.known-extra: Does their age change their height? You don't need that number.
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: 11 cm shorter. What don't we know?
feedback.sentence-empty: Fill every gap in both sentences.
feedback.sentence-box: We don't know Ahmad's height. Put one box □ there.
feedback.sentence-numbers: The first sentence uses the easy numbers (150 and 10), the second the real ones (147 and 11).
feedback.sentence-false: "Shorter" means Ahmad's height is less than Reza's. Change the sign.
feedback.solve-empty: Type the number in the box after "□ =".
feedback.solve-wrong: Work out the number in the box again.
feedback.added: Ahmad is shorter, so his height must be less than 147.
feedback.simple-answer: 140 was the answer to the simpler problem. Give the answer to the second sentence.
feedback.too-big: Look at the answer to the second sentence.
feedback.too-small: Look at the answer to the second sentence.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

list-numbers.title: A systematic list: two-digit numbers
list-numbers.prompt: Write every two-digit number whose tens digit is 5 or 7 and whose ones digit is 3, 4 or 8. How many are there? Work in order: first all the numbers with 5 tens.
list-numbers.hint: Put 5 tens with each of the three ones digits: 53, 54, 58. Then do 7 tens. If you run out of rows, tap "add a row".
list-numbers.why: Without writing them all, how could you tell there are 6 numbers?
list-numbers.model: Each tens digit makes one number with each of the 3 ones digits. 5 tens gives three numbers and 7 tens gives three: 3 + 3 = 6, or 2 × 3 = 6. Because I worked in order, I didn't miss any.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need: the tens digits and the ones digits both matter.
feedback.known-extra: Does the colour of the cards change the numbers?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: the tens digit is 5 or 7. What don't we know?
feedback.table-empty: In the table, write the tens digit and the ones digit of each number.
feedback.list-wrong: One of the numbers breaks the rule. Tens can only be 5 or 7, ones only 3, 4 or 8.
feedback.list-repeat: You have written one number twice. Each number only once.
feedback.list-missing: Some numbers are still missing. For each tens digit, write all three ones digits.
feedback.missed-one: Count the rows of the table again.
feedback.missed-two: Count the rows of the table again. Each tens digit gives three numbers.
feedback.too-big: Count only the rows of the table.
feedback.too-small: Count only the rows of the table.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

choose-strategy.title: Choose your own strategy
choose-strategy.prompt: Fatima has 3 times as many stamps as Ali. Together they have 24 stamps. How many stamps does Ali have? Choose a strategy: draw a picture, or guess and check.
choose-strategy.hint: Draw: Ali's stamps are one part and Fatima's are 3 parts the same size; how many equal parts altogether? Guess and check: guess a number for Ali.
choose-strategy.success: Well done! Ali has 6 stamps and Fatima has 3 × 6 = 18. 6 + 18 = 24.
choose-strategy.why: Which strategy did you choose? Why was it a good way for this problem?
choose-strategy.model: Drawing: Ali has 1 part and Fatima 3 parts, 4 equal parts altogether. 24 ÷ 4 = 6, so each part is 6. Guess and check: if Ali had 5, together they would have 20 (too few); with 6 they have 24. Both ways give the same answer.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need: "3 times as many" and "24 together" both matter.
feedback.known-extra: Does Fatima's age change the number of stamps?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: 24 together. What don't we know?
feedback.strategy-empty: Choose a strategy: draw a picture, or guess and check.
feedback.fatima: 18 is Fatima's stamps. The question asks about Ali.
feedback.three-parts: 24 ÷ 3 = 8, but there aren't 3 parts: Ali has 1 part and Fatima 3, so 4 parts altogether.
feedback.minus-three: "3 times as many" means three lots of Ali's stamps, not 3 more.
feedback.too-big: Test your answer: Ali's stamps and 3 times as many make more than 24.
feedback.too-small: Test your answer: Ali's stamps and 3 times as many don't reach 24.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.
